blogs.title: Speeding up language models for travel applications
blogs.author: Daniel Zagyva, Laurens van der Maas
blogs.description: Two optimization techniques, when combined, can significantly improve a model’s speed and cost effectiveness without sacrificing quality.
blogs.content: Conversational AI Speeding up language models for travel applications Two optimization techniques, when combined, can significantly improve a model’s speed and cost effectiveness without sacrificing quality. By Daniel Zagyva , Laurens van der Maas October 29, 2026 5 min read Share Share Copy link Email X LinkedIn Facebook Line Reddit QZone Sina Weibo WeChat WhatsApp 分享到微信 x Listen • 7:25 min Key takeaways Combining knowledge distillation (KD) with the Medusa-2 framework produced a final model (TinyLlama at 1.1 billion parameters) that matched the quality of the 70-billion-parameter Llama-3.1 teacher while running 10 to 20 times as fast. For Booking.com's Smart Filters, the KD-plus-Medusa approach delivered responses 15 times as fast for 99% of queries; knowledge distillation alone closed the student-teacher quality gap by more than 90% and made inference roughly six times as fast, after which Medusa heads added a further 2 to 3.6× speedup. On the two remaining use cases, the pipeline drove a 2.9% increase in user engagement for the AI Trip Planner (vs. GPT-3.5) and 1.4% more "helpful" ratings for AI-generated accommodation descriptions at lower costs than other models. Was this answer helpful? Travel platforms serve millions of daily users by answering questions about destinations, offering hotel recommendations, and helping users plan their trips. In recent years, many platforms have turned to large language models (LLMs) to improve these services. The LLMs give accurate, contextually relevant travel advice thanks to their size: they typically have tens of billions of parameters. Unfortunately, such large models are also computationally expensive, and that expense scales with the number of customer queries. What’s more, such large models can be too slow for web and mobile applications, where a delay of even 100 milliseconds can cost a company customers and revenue. To address these scaling and latency challenges, we explored two complementary optimization techniques. One is a compression technique known as knowledge distillation (KD), in which a slow but powerful model produces training targets for a faster, lightweight model. The other, called Medusa , is a framework that transforms sequential next-token predictions — a common bottleneck in LLMs — into parallel computations. Working with leading online travel agency Booking.com, we applied KD and Medusa techniques to the LLMs that power various aspects of its user experience, looking to improve either latency or cost effectiveness. We focused on three features in particular: The AI Trip Planner: A conversational assistant that must extract travel preferences from dialogue in less than a second (latency); Smart Filters: A feature that converts natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time (latency); Accommodation Description Generation: A feature that produces property descriptions on the scale of millions of listings (cost effectiveness). We demonstrated that combining both KD and Medusa maintains the quality of the best open-source LLMs at less than one-third the cost while running up to 20 times as fast. Our framework ensures that travel platforms or other applications that rely on LLMs can deliver fast, cost-effective, accurate responses in real-world scenarios. We presented these techniques at last year’s meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), where it received the Industry Track best-paper award. LLM-powered Smart Filters convert natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time. Our approach: Medusa plus knowledge distillation Medusa is a framework designed to reduce LLM latency in real-time applications such as chat and code generation. It improves computational efficiency at run time — inference time — rather than during training. Ordinarily, an LLM generates text one token — word or word part — at a time. Medusa accelerates this process by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. Medusa does this by adding prediction modules, called Medusa heads, to the base LLM, one head for each token decoded in parallel. GPU hardware that LLMs run on is optimized for parallelism, so it can handle parallel token decoding with little additional overhead. Medusa offers significant speedups, typically 2-4-fold without compromising generation quality. Knowledge distillation addresses the deployment challenges of large, parameter-heavy models by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models to smaller “student” models. Typically, a teacher model is first trained or fine-tuned on high-quality labeled data, then used to generate predictions on additional unlabeled data. The manually labeled and machine-labeled data are then combined to train a smaller student model, which learns to mimic the teacher’s behavior. The student model retains much of the teacher’s performance but is significantly more efficient, making it better suited for real-world scenarios such as high-volume consumer-facing websites. In our work, we integrate KD and Medusa in a unified pipeline starting with pretrained base models. As in standard KD, we fine-tune the teacher on the labeled dataset and use it to generate predictions on unlabeled, domain-relevant text. During the student-training stage, however, we attach Medusa heads to the student model and train it on the combined corpus of teacher predictions and labeled data. This produces a single compact model that inherits the teacher's knowledge while also gaining multitoken-prediction capabilities. The experiment We chose TinyLlama — a compact model with 1.1 billion parameters — as our student and Llama-3.1 with 70 billion parameters as the teacher. We ran four progressive experiments, each building on the last. We first fine-tuned TinyLlama on task-specific data for each of our three use cases — AI trip planning, smart filtering, and accommodation description generation. Even without further optimization, the fine-tuned models were significantly more accurate than few-shot GPT-4o, confirming that domain-specific fine tuning compensates for their compact size. However, their performance still fell short of the much larger teacher model’s. Applying knowledge distillation — training the student on a blend of human-annotated and teacher-annotated data — closed that gap by more than 90%, bringing the small model to near parity with the teacher. The smaller model size also made inference roughly 6 times as fast, but that’s still not fast enough for real-time use. Adding Medusa heads, however, sped up inference an additional 2 to 3.6 times. We tested two Medusa variants: with Medusa-1, we first fine-tuned the base LLM, then froze its weights and fine-tuned the Medusa heads separately; with Medusa-2, we trained everything in a single stage. Both achieved comparable speedups with no meaningful quality loss, but Medusa-2's simpler pipeline made it more practical for production teams managing multiple models. Outcomes Combining KD with Medusa-2 delivered both gains simultaneously: our final model matched the quality of the 70-billion-parameter teacher while running 10 to 20 times as fast, depending on the use case. For each of the three use cases, we used the pipeline described above to fine-tune a dedicated model with domain-specific data. For AI Trip Planner, we showed a 2.9% increase in user engagement vs. GPT-3.5. For Smart Filters, we achieved responses that were 15 times as fast for 99 percent of queries. For AI-generated accommodation descriptions, we showed 1.4% more “helpful” ratings from users, at less than one-third the cost of GPT-4. With acknowledgements to our AWS colleague Aleksandra Dokic and to the Booking.com team: Emmanouil Stergiadis, Eran Fainman, Ilya Gusev, and Moran Beladev . Research areas Conversational AI Search and information retrieval Tags Large language models (LLMs) About the Author Daniel Zagyva Daniel Zagyva is a senior machine learning engineer at Amazon Web Services (AWS). Laurens van der Maas Laurens van der Maas is a senior applied scientist with Amazon Web Services (AWS).

Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity, a centralized directory for discovering and installing third-party and Google-built plugins across the Antigravity App and the Antigravity CLI. Until now, connecting an agent to external systems meant manually configuring Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints, environment variables, domain skills, and custom subagents across individual repositories or local configuration files. The Plugin Marketplace packages these primitives into verified, shareable bundles that you can browse by category and install in a click. Instead of switching between browser tabs to look up a ticket, inspect a design spec, query production logs, or check a security alert, you can give your agent direct, scoped access to the systems where your team already works. As Antigravity continues to optimize for builders, we are launching the marketplace with integrations from partners across software delivery, enterprise operations, data analytics, design, commerce, and security. Here is a look at what each launch partner brings to your workflow in Antigravity. What are the components of a plugin? An Antigravity plugin is a versioned, self-contained bundle defined by a plugin.json manifest. Rather than configuring tools and instructions piece by piece across individual repositories, a plugin packages up to five extensibility primitives that install, update, and toggle on or off together as a single unit. Skills Skills are modular packages of domain knowledge, multi-step procedures, and optional helper scripts defined in a SKILL.md file. While tools give an agent raw access to an external system, skills teach the agent how to sequence those tools reliably for complex workflows such as incident triage, schema migration, or design-to-code translation. To keep the agent’s context window focused, Antigravity uses progressive disclosure: only each skill’s name and short description are loaded at startup, and the full instructions, reference docs, and scripts are pulled into context on demand when relevant to your prompt or invoked via a /skill-name slash command. MCP Servers Model Context Protocol (MCP) server configurations ( mcp.json ) connect the agent to external APIs, databases, and developer tools over remote Streamable HTTP endpoints or local standard input/output ( stdio ) processes. Plugins can declare required user variables (such as API tokens or workspace URLs) or OAuth 2.0 authentication flows, prompting you once during setup in the Antigravity UI or CLI and automatically scoping tool availability to the plugin’s lifecycle. Rules Rules are Markdown instructions ( rules/AGENTS.md or rules/*.md ) that establish persistent guardrails, coding conventions, API usage constraints, and domain standards. Rules bundled inside a plugin can remain active whenever the plugin is enabled or load dynamically when the agent determines they are relevant to the task at hand, ensuring the agent follows organizational policies and partner best practices such as query cost limits, SDK conventions, or read-only operational modes. Hooks Lifecycle hooks ( hooks.json ) execute deterministic shell commands or scripts at specific points in the agent’s execution loop, including SessionStart , PreToolUse , PostToolUse , PreInvocation , PostInvocation , and Stop . Because hooks run outside the model’s reasoning loop and exchange structured JSON over standard input and output, teams can use them to gate or block sensitive tool calls, redact secrets from tool outputs, inject workspace context at startup, or require linters and test suites to pass before the agent finishes a turn. Custom Agents Custom agents ( agents/<agent-name>.md ) define specialized personas and subagents with tailored system prompts, curated tool allowlists, model selections, and command execution policies. A custom agent bundled in a plugin can be selected as the primary session agent for a dedicated workflow or spawned in the background by the main agent to handle focused tasks, such as a security posture audit, log investigation, or code review, in an isolated context window. Plugins to explore Productivity & Project Management Atlassian Atlassian Teamwork Graph CLI is Atlassian’s agent-first interface to your entire work context: Jira issues, Confluence pages, Bitbucket PRs, along with your connected third-party data sources. Design, Creative & Media Canva Generate new visual designs from text prompts, review existing layouts, automatically resize assets across social and presentation formats, and validate designs against organizational Brand Kits using the Canva MCP server and design skills. Developer Tools CrowdStrike Connect Antigravity to the CrowdStrike Falcon platform through the CrowdStrike MCP server to triage detections, research threat intelligence, prioritize vulnerabilities, research identities, and more using natural-language prompts. Business Databricks Connect Antigravity to your Databricks environment so agents can ask Genie for trusted, semantically driven answers, execute queries against SQL warehouses, and accelerate notebook, app, and pipeline development, all governed through Unity Catalog permissions. Developer Tools Datadog Search and act on your Datadog data. Debug production with logs, traces, monitors, and incidents, then trace the problem back to your code and get a suggested fix. Productivity & Project Management Dropbox Connect Antigravity to Dropbox to search and organize files and folders, inspect metadata, and turn documents into actionable context for seamless collaboration. Design, Creative & Media Figma The Figma MCP server brings Figma into your AI workflow. It gives AI agents the design context they need to generate code from your Figma files, and lets agents write native Figma content back to the canvas. Productivity & Project Management monday.com Connect Antigravity to your monday.com AI workspaces through the official monday.com MCP server and deliver better outcomes faster and smarter, across every use case. Developer Tools Ping Identity Configure and monitor your PingOne environments without leaving Antigravity. Built on Ping Identity’s AI-first headless identity foundation, the plugin combines the PingOne remote MCP server and bundled skills so agents can inspect applications, users, and sign-on policies while helping you seamlessly build identity into your apps. Developer Tools SentinelOne Query your SentinelOne Singularity Console through the read-only Purple AI MCP server to investigate alerts, run PowerQueries on event data, track vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, and ask Purple AI security questions without leaving Antigravity. Business Stripe Connect Antigravity to your Stripe account through the Stripe MCP server to look up customers, payments, and subscriptions, search Stripe documentation, and build or debug payment integrations. Developer Tools Unity Connect Unity to Antigravity in a single click to build, simulate, and manage real-time 3D development workflows. Getting started The Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity is rolling out today across the Antigravity App and the Antigravity CLI. To explore the catalog and install your first plugin, open the Customizations panel in the Antigravity App and browse the Plugins tab, or install plugins directly from your terminal using agy plugin install <plugin-name> : agy plugin install < plugin-nam e > To learn how to build and package your own plugins for your team or the community, check out the Plugins documentation and the Marketplace guide . Before publishing or sharing a plugin, you can validate its plugin.json manifest and MCP server configurations and test it locally from your terminal: # Validate plugin.json and MCP server configurations agy plugin validate ./ < plugin-nam e > # Install and test the plugin locally from your working directory agy plugin install ./ < plugin-nam e > # Verify the plugin is installed and enabled agy plugin list If you are a technology partner interested in publishing an official integration in the Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity, validate your plugin bundle and submit your details through the partner interest form . blogs.name: IBM Research Blog
blogs.title: How Zurich is shaping the future of algorithms, 70 years in
blogs.author: Mariana Rajado Silva
blogs.description: As IBM’s Zurich Lab turns 70, director Alessandro Curioni speaks about the celebrations, his work on Algorithms & Applications, and his vision for the future.
blogs.content: Forty years ago, when Alessandro Curioni was a high school student, he was watching the news on Italian television as they announced the Physics Nobel Prize of 1986. It went to researchers Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at the IBM Research Lab in Zurich for their invention of the scanning tunneling microscope , a device that has since revolutionized the field of nanotechnology. The way the researchers talked about their invention stuck with Curioni, but he was even more struck by how they spoke about the lab where they worked: a powerful innovation hub, buzzing with people and ideas. This image stayed with him, and many years later, while working on his Ph.D. in computational chemistry in Pisa, he became aware of the research being conducted at the Zurich lab on advanced computational molecular simulation methods. This was one of the only two places worldwide where unique, groundbreaking work was being done on Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics. If he did not learn these new, more advanced techniques, Curioni reasoned, his Ph.D. work would be incomplete. After talking to his Ph.D. advisor, Curioni came to Zurich. When he first arrived, his goal was to learn these methods for his thesis and leave for California, where the technological explosion of the ‘80s and ‘90s was taking place. But somewhere along the way, this buzzing lab in the middle of Europe, filled with experts in a wide range of disciplines from so many corners of the world, changed his mind. These researchers were attempting to solve some of the biggest problems in science and business, with an eye toward tackling important challenges and delivering meaningful impact. There was no better place to do just that. Upon the 70th anniversary of the Zurich lab, we sat down with Curioni to talk about how he landed there, how the vibrant research ecosystem surrounding the lab made him decide to stay, and his vision for the future of computing. This interview has been edited for clarity and length. How did you celebrate the recent 70th anniversary of the IBM Research Lab in Zurich? We had the great pleasure of hosting two distinct events: an evening anniversary celebration on October 12, and a client-devoted symposium on October 13. For the anniversary celebration, our audience consisted of key figures from the scientific, industrial and political realms in Europe, as well as key media representatives. We had the honor of hosting a number of IBM’s clients and partners, several of them also former IBMers, and even Physics Nobel Laureate Georg Bednorz , who was a member of the Zurich lab in 1987 when he was recognized for his discovery of high-temperature superconductivity. At the anniversary celebration, we watched wonderful video messages by IBM’s CEO and Chairman Arvind Krisha, as well as by the president of Switzerland. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, gave an inspiring keynote, followed by comments from the president of ETH, one of Europe’s top universities. We also held a panel discussion with the president of EPFL (another key Swiss university), the Director-General of CERN, and the head of Deep Tech at Nestlé R&D. Lastly, the president of the ETH Board shared some closing remarks before we all gathered at the Think Lab for dinner. Alessandro Curioni gives the opening keynote at the anniversary celebration on Oct 12. The symposium was designed as a smaller, technology-focused event. We invited many of IBM’s clients and partners, and our goal was to spark powerful dialogue and share our vision for the future of computing. After a keynote by Gambetta, some of our lead researchers had the pleasure of sharing the stage with several of our partners: Bosch, Cleveland Clinic, Dallara, E.ON, JPMorgan Chase, and Threema. It was wonderful to host these celebration events — especially with our collaborators and clients in attendance. Through the many inspiring speeches and presentations we witnessed, I think we all realized how exceptional the IBM Research Lab in Zurich is, how much groundbreaking innovation is being done in the Zurich area, and how we are keen on continuing to shape the world of technology for much, much longer. It was more than 10 years ago that I took over the leadership of this lab. Overall, I have a feeling that I have made this place even more connected to the future of computing, to the needs of the company, and to the overall tech ecosystem — and that makes me tremendously proud. What do you see as the key aspects driving success at IBM Research? The first factor I would highlight is our ability to attract top talent, both in Zurich and beyond. If you take a look at similar organizations — even though a concept truly similar to IBM Research cannot quite be found elsewhere — there is a lot of staff turnover. Employees come and go. At IBM Research, once someone arrives, it’s unlikely that they will leave (unless, of course, they choose to for personal reasons). I would call that a culture of innovation done right: ethical, transformative technological development that follows market demand while keeping skilled people engaged. The second key aspect is the global character of this organization. IBM Research has talent from almost every place on Earth, and our impact knows no borders. Many of our remarkable collaborators are giants in their country or even in their continent — but their reach ends there. IBM Research is a global enterprise. Our ability to marry research with the corporate world is unprecedented, and that makes us unique — and hence able to bring remarkable value to all corners of this Earth. Aerial view of the IBM Research Zurich campus. You’re leading IBM Research’s efforts on Algorithms and Applications. Can you tell us more about the work being done in this area? Algorithms play a key role in computing. One can have extremely powerful, advanced hardware, but without the key layer of algorithms, it is simply not possible to extract trusted value from it. At IBM Research, we are creating foundational algorithms that combine classical computing, quantum computing, and AI. We are focusing on five broad problem classes: differential equations and dynamical systems; linear algebra and Hamiltonian problems; optimization and combinatorial problems; probability, statistics, and stochastic processes; and cryptography. We believe that, by tackling these five areas, our results will cover a large percentage of today’s most urgent challenges. AI and quantum play key roles here — the former provides us new abstractions, and the latter brings us new representations. I firmly believe that the future of computing will be defined by the joint use of CPUs, GPUs, QPUs, and an agentic AI layer for orchestration. The synergistic use of these technologies will lead us to fundamentally new ways of approaching complex problems, and hence allow us to reach unprecedented solutions. What is your vision for the future of computing? Being a computational scientist by training, my dream was always to use a computer to simulate the world and all of its phenomena, from the scientific to the industrial realms. I would say there is no better moment in history to do this. The algorithms we are creating can translate technology into tangible value. We are creating a future where, on the one hand, we can do what we have done before in better, faster, and more efficient ways, and, on the other hand, we can do things that have simply been out of reach until now. For the very first time, we have the ability to create extremely accurate digital twins of our world, both in science and business — and that capability is invaluable. Researching algorithms has always been central to my life, but today I find it is more meaningful than ever. Being part of an organization that is leading the connection between technology and societal value is tremendously exciting. The future of computing looks promising, and I am very proud to keep shaping it at IBM Research.
